government.name: City of Port Moody
government.howBuilt: This list draws on 2026 campaign coverage of Port Moody's mayor and council races from the Tri-Cities Dispatch, Freshet News, The Tyee and the Tri-City News, candidate statements on VoteMate, and recent City of Port Moody council decisions on the budget, the community plan, housing, parks and transportation, as listed in each issue's sources. We kept issues council can act on through its plans, zoning, budget and services. Issues are not ranked by importance.

issues.title: Housing costs and supply
issues.description: How many homes get built in Port Moody, what kinds they are, and how many are priced below market, at a time when the city says most new projects cannot currently meet its 15% below-market target.
issues.whatItAffects: Renters, first-time buyers, seniors, families looking for larger units, and people who work in Port Moody.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets zoning, density bonus rules and affordable-housing requirements for new projects, and can partner with BC Housing or use city land; provincial housing laws limit some of these tools.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city approach new housing?
viewQuestion.poleA: Approve more homes, including taller buildings near SkyTrain, and accept fewer below-market units when projects would otherwise stall
viewQuestion.poleB: Approve fewer, more family-sized homes and hold firmer on below-market requirements, even if fewer projects go ahead

tradeoffs.context: Housing choices trade how many homes get built against how many are affordable and suited to families.

gains: More homes could be built sooner, which may ease rents and prices
Projects may be more likely to proceed in a slow market
costs: Fewer new units may be priced below market
Many new units may be small and less suited to families

gains: More new units could suit families, seniors and lower incomes
Affordability targets may stay clearer and more predictable
costs: Fewer projects may go ahead, slowing new supply
Rents and prices could stay higher for longer

issues.title: Growth and the community plan
issues.description: How much and how fast Port Moody grows under its new official community plan, which concentrates towers near the Moody Centre and Inlet Centre SkyTrain stations, including recently approved 39-storey towers.
issues.whatItAffects: All residents, especially those living near SkyTrain stations, plus future residents and local businesses.
issues.whoDecides: Council adopts and amends the official community plan and votes on rezonings; provincial transit-oriented rules require it to allow certain densities near SkyTrain.

viewQuestion.question: How should Port Moody manage growth over the next few years?
viewQuestion.poleA: Keep the current plan, with tall buildings near SkyTrain that bring new homes, shops and developer-funded amenities
viewQuestion.poleB: Revisit the plan to slow growth and favour mid-size buildings, keeping more land for jobs and parks

tradeoffs.context: Growth choices trade new homes and amenities near transit against the pace of change in the city.

gains: More homes, shops and jobs may locate near SkyTrain
Developer contributions could help fund new amenities
costs: Traffic, schools and services may face more pressure
Neighbourhood scale and views may change noticeably

gains: Change may come at a pace residents find easier to absorb
More land could stay available for jobs and parks
costs: Fewer new homes could keep housing costs higher
Revisions may take time and may conflict with provincial rules

issues.title: Getting around the city
issues.description: Traffic on St. Johns Street, Murray Street and the busy St. Johns overpass near Ioco Road, and how much road space goes to cars versus walking and cycling.
issues.whatItAffects: Drivers, commuters, transit riders, cyclists, pedestrians and businesses along St. Johns Street.
issues.whoDecides: Council decides city road designs, lane use, parking and pathway projects, and works with TransLink, which funds and approves some regional road and transit work.

viewQuestion.question: What should the city prioritize on its busiest streets?
viewQuestion.poleA: Add road capacity for cars, such as extra lanes and a wider overpass, to ease congestion
viewQuestion.poleB: Put more into walking, cycling and transit routes so fewer trips need a car

tradeoffs.context: Street choices trade quicker relief for drivers against longer-term shifts toward other ways of travelling.

gains: Drivers may see shorter delays at busy pinch points
Road projects can be faster and cheaper to deliver
costs: Added lanes may fill up again as traffic grows
Less space or money may go to walking and cycling

gains: More people may choose to walk, cycle or take transit
Streets could become safer and calmer for all users
costs: Drivers may face continued congestion in the short term
Benefits may depend on transit service the city does not control

issues.title: Property taxes and city spending
issues.description: How much Port Moody raises property taxes and what it funds, after a 2026 budget that started at an 8.65% proposed increase and was cut to a provisional 4.25%.
issues.whatItAffects: Homeowners, renters (through rents), businesses, and everyone who uses city services, police and facilities.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets the annual budget and tax rate, decides service levels, fees such as paid parking, and how much to put into reserves for aging infrastructure.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city balance taxes and services?
viewQuestion.poleA: Keep tax increases low by trimming services, events or new projects
viewQuestion.poleB: Accept higher tax increases to maintain services and keep up with infrastructure and new facilities

tradeoffs.context: Budget choices trade lower tax bills against the level of services and upkeep the city can fund.

gains: Households and businesses may face smaller tax increases
Spending may be held to core needs
costs: Some services, events or projects could be reduced or delayed
Deferred upkeep may cost more later

gains: Services and community programs may be maintained
Infrastructure reserves could stay healthier over time
costs: Tax bills may rise faster for owners and, indirectly, renters
Higher costs may add to cost-of-living pressures

issues.title: Parks and the waterfront
issues.description: Whether and how to expand Rocky Point Park and upgrade the waterfront, including a $43-million park master plan and debate over the neighbouring Flavelle mill site.
issues.whatItAffects: Park users, families, downtown residents, waterfront businesses and visitors.
issues.whoDecides: Council approves park plans and budgets, can buy land, and sets the land-use designation of nearby sites in the community plan.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city improve its waterfront parks?
viewQuestion.poleA: Focus on upgrading the existing park space to make more of it usable
viewQuestion.poleB: Focus on acquiring more land to make the park physically larger

tradeoffs.context: Park choices trade improving the space the city already has against buying more land for a larger park.

gains: Upgrades may reach residents sooner and at a known cost
More of the existing park could become usable year-round
costs: The park's total size may not grow with the population
Crowding may continue at busy times

gains: A larger park may better serve a growing downtown
More waterfront could be kept as public space long term
costs: Land purchase and cleanup could be very costly
Timing may depend on private owners and negotiations

issues.title: Recreation and community facilities
issues.description: Plans to replace the aging Kyle Centre with a new community centre, plaza and larger park, estimated at $30 million to $40 million, and broader demand for recreation space as the city grows.
issues.whatItAffects: Seniors, families, arts and recreation users, and taxpayers who would help fund new buildings.
issues.whoDecides: Council decides which facilities to build or renovate, their size and timing, and how to pay through reserves, borrowing, grants or developer fees.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city approach its community facilities?
viewQuestion.poleA: Build new, larger facilities now to serve a growing population, even at a higher cost
viewQuestion.poleB: Renovate and maintain existing facilities to keep costs and borrowing lower

tradeoffs.context: Facility choices trade more space for a growing city against the cost and borrowing needed to build it.

gains: More programmable space may meet growing demand
New buildings may be more efficient and accessible
costs: Construction costs and debt may raise property taxes
Costs could rise above early estimates

gains: Upfront costs and borrowing may stay lower
Existing facilities could keep serving users with less disruption
costs: Space may fall short as the population grows
Older buildings may need more repairs over time

issues.title: Child care
issues.description: How the city helps add child care spaces, including a proposed modular daycare at city hall and ideas to require child care space in new buildings.
issues.whatItAffects: Parents of young children, child care workers, employers and city staff.
issues.whoDecides: Council can build or lease space for child care on city land, set zoning and development requirements, and apply for provincial grants; licensing and fee subsidies are provincial.

viewQuestion.question: What role should the city play in child care?
viewQuestion.poleA: Have the city build and own child care spaces directly on city land
viewQuestion.poleB: Have the city encourage child care mainly through development rules and partners, rather than building it

tradeoffs.context: Child care choices trade direct city involvement against relying on partners and development rules.

gains: Spaces may be delivered on city land with more city control
City-run spaces could help recruit and keep staff
costs: The city may take on building and operating costs
City land used for child care may not be available for other uses

gains: Costs may fall more on developers and operators than taxpayers
Spaces could be spread across new buildings citywide
costs: Spaces may arrive more slowly and less predictably
The city may have less say over fees and access

issues.title: Local jobs and industry
issues.description: How much land Port Moody keeps for industry and employment, including heavy industrial sites and former industrial land near SkyTrain, as industrial taxes have fallen to about 15% of city revenue.
issues.whatItAffects: Workers, local businesses, industrial operators, nearby residents, and taxpayers.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets land-use designations and zoning for industrial and commercial land, and decides whether to allow those lands to be redeveloped for housing.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city use land that has been industrial?
viewQuestion.poleA: Protect and expand industrial and job space to support jobs and the business tax base
viewQuestion.poleB: Allow some industrial land to become mixed housing and commercial areas near transit

tradeoffs.context: Land choices trade keeping space for jobs and business taxes against using land for housing near transit.

gains: Local jobs and the business tax base may be protected
Residents may have more options to work close to home
costs: Less land may be available for new housing
Conflicts over noise and odours near homes may continue

gains: More homes and shops could be built near transit
Redeveloped sites may bring new amenities and activity
costs: Some job space and industrial tax revenue could be lost
Fewer local jobs may mean longer commutes

issues.title: Public input and how council decides
issues.description: How much weight council gives resident feedback on big decisions such as the community plan and tower approvals, alongside debate over the city's first municipal party and campaign donations.
issues.whatItAffects: All residents, community groups, developers, and candidates.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets its own consultation processes, public hearing practices and meeting rules; campaign finance rules are set by the province.

viewQuestion.question: How should council make major decisions?
viewQuestion.poleA: Give residents a larger, more direct say, such as more consultation or votes, before major decisions
viewQuestion.poleB: Rely on elected councillors to decide after standard consultation, so decisions stay timely

tradeoffs.context: Decision-making choices trade broader resident involvement against the speed and clarity of decisions.

gains: Residents may feel more heard and trust decisions more
Concerns could be raised earlier in the process
costs: Decisions may take longer and cost more to reach
Louder or better-organized groups may carry more weight

gains: Decisions may be made faster and more predictably
Elected councillors may stay clearly accountable at elections
costs: Some residents may feel left out of major choices
Disagreements may surface later, after decisions are made

election.name: City of Port Moody general local election

locations: Port Moody Recreation Complex (Wellness Room), 300 Ioco Road
Port Moody Recreation Complex (Wellness Room), 300 Ioco Road

election.howToVote: Port Moody voters can vote at any of four locations on General Voting Day (Saturday, Oct. 17, 8 a.m.-8 p.m.): Port Moody Recreation Complex Gymnasium (300 Ioco Road), Kyle Centre (125 Kyle Street), Heritage Mountain Community Centre (200 Panorama Place) or Glenayre Community Centre (492 Glencoe Drive); at advance voting Oct. 7 or Oct. 10; or by mail ballot. Voters choose up to one mayor, six councillors and two school trustees. The City uses the provincial voters list; voters not registered can register when they vote by showing two documents that together prove identity and residence, at least one with a signature. Non-resident property electors must also register with the City and bring proof of property ownership. Voting places are accessible and curbside voting is available.
election.voteByMail: All qualified resident and non-resident property electors may vote by mail. Apply online, by PDF dropped off at City Hall (100 Newport Drive) or in person by 12 p.m. (noon) Friday, Oct. 9, 2026. Ballots must be received by 8 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026: by mail to the Chief Election Officer, at the City Hall counter or 24-hour drop box, at Kyle Centre (Oct. 5-16, 8:30 a.m.-4 p.m.), or at any voting place during voting. Unregistered voters must include a completed registration form with copies of two IDs and a witness signature. The municipal mail ballot is separate from the Oct. 24 provincial election.

government.name: School District 43 (Coquitlam)
government.howBuilt: This list draws on statements from Port Moody's 2026 school trustee candidates reported by Freshet News, SD43 board meeting minutes and budget releases, and news coverage of school planning, safety and funding in the Tri-Cities, as listed in each issue's sources. Issues focus on what the SD43 board can do and how it affects Port Moody students. Issues are not ranked by importance.

issues.title: District budget and funding
issues.description: How SD43 balances its budget when it says provincial grants have not kept up with rising costs, while enrolment and international student revenue came in below forecasts.
issues.whatItAffects: Students, teachers, support staff, and families across Port Moody, Coquitlam, Port Coquitlam, Anmore and Belcarra.
issues.whoDecides: The board adopts the annual budget and decides where to cut or spend, but most funding is set by the province and the board must balance its budget.

viewQuestion.question: How should the board handle tight budgets?
viewQuestion.poleA: Protect classroom staffing and supports first, and cut elsewhere, such as administration or extra programs
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep a broad mix of programs and services, and accept leaner staffing or larger reductions in some areas

tradeoffs.context: Budget choices trade protecting classroom staffing against keeping a wider range of programs and services.

gains: Class sizes and direct student supports may be protected
Spending may stay focused on core teaching
costs: Some programs or services outside classrooms could be cut
Administrative capacity may be stretched

gains: Students may keep access to a broad mix of programs
Services that families rely on may continue
costs: Classroom staffing may become leaner
Reductions may be spread in ways that are harder to see

issues.title: Planning schools for growth
issues.description: Where and when SD43 plans new schools as Port Moody adds thousands of homes, including a proposed school site at the Flavelle mill waterfront that Port Moody council first rejected and then accepted in 2025.
issues.whatItAffects: Families in growing neighbourhoods, students at crowded schools, and city and district taxpayers.
issues.whoDecides: The board proposes school sites and capital projects and asks the province for funding; the city must accept the site plan, and the province decides which projects get built.

viewQuestion.question: How should the district plan for new schools?
viewQuestion.poleA: Secure school sites early, before new neighbourhoods are built, even if some plans change
viewQuestion.poleB: Wait for confirmed development and enrolment before committing to new school sites

tradeoffs.context: School planning choices trade securing sites early against waiting for clearer growth and enrolment.

gains: Schools may be ready closer to when families move in
Land may be secured before prices or options change
costs: Sites may be planned for developments that change or stall
Early plans may cause friction with cities and landowners

gains: Plans may better match actual development and enrolment
Fewer resources may be spent on sites never used
costs: Students may face crowding or portables while schools catch up
Suitable land may be harder or costlier to find later

issues.title: Support for diverse learners
issues.description: How SD43 supports a growing number of students with disabilities or diverse needs and English language learners, after adding 42 education assistant positions in 2025-26.
issues.whatItAffects: Students with diverse needs, English language learners, their families, teachers and education assistants.
issues.whoDecides: The board decides how much of its budget goes to education assistants, specialist teachers and support services, within provincial funding and policy.

viewQuestion.question: How should the district support students with extra learning needs?
viewQuestion.poleA: Add more education assistants and specialist staff, even if it means less funding elsewhere
viewQuestion.poleB: Hold support staffing steady and focus on training and classroom strategies for all teachers

tradeoffs.context: Support choices trade adding specialized staff against spreading resources across all classrooms.

gains: Students with extra needs may get more one-on-one help
Teachers may have more hands-on support in class
costs: Less funding may be left for other programs
Staff may be hard to hire in a tight labour market

gains: Budgets may stay steadier for other priorities
Training may help teachers support all students
costs: Some students may get less individual help
Teacher workload may stay high in complex classrooms

issues.title: School safety and student well-being
issues.description: How SD43 keeps schools safe and supports student well-being, after threatening calls led to hold-and-secure lockdowns at Tri-Cities schools, including Port Moody's Glenayre Elementary, in early 2026, and concerns about youth vaping.
issues.whatItAffects: Students, parents, school staff and local police.
issues.whoDecides: The board sets district safety, emergency and student-conduct policies and funds counselling and well-being programs; police handle criminal threats.

viewQuestion.question: Where should the district focus on safety and well-being?
viewQuestion.poleA: Put more into physical security, emergency preparedness and clear rules
viewQuestion.poleB: Put more into counselling, mental health and prevention programs

tradeoffs.context: Safety choices trade investment in security and rules against investment in prevention and mental health.

gains: Schools may respond faster and more consistently in emergencies
Clear rules may help families know what to expect
costs: Less funding may be left for counselling and prevention
Some students may feel schools are less welcoming

gains: Students may get help earlier, before problems grow
Supports may address causes such as stress or vaping
costs: Physical security upgrades may be slower
Results may take longer to show and be harder to measure

issues.title: Child care at schools
issues.description: Whether SD43 should use school space and buildings for child care, such as the planned conversion of Port Moody's vacant Ioco School into a child care centre.
issues.whatItAffects: Parents of young and school-aged children, child care providers and schools short on space.
issues.whoDecides: The board decides whether to offer school space or buildings for child care and applies for provincial grants; the province sets child care funding and licensing.

viewQuestion.question: What role should the district play in child care?
viewQuestion.poleA: Make more school space and buildings available for child care and before- and after-school care
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep school space focused on classrooms and leave child care mainly to other providers

tradeoffs.context: Child care choices trade convenient care on school grounds against keeping school space for classrooms.

gains: Families may get care at the same site as school
Unused or older buildings could be put to good use
costs: Space may be needed for classrooms as enrolment grows
District staff time and costs may rise

gains: School space may stay available for classes and programs
The district may stay focused on education
costs: Families may face fewer or less convenient care options
Child care may be harder to find near schools

issues.title: Specialized programs and career pathways
issues.description: How much SD43 invests in programs of choice and career pathways, such as dual-credit trades training with post-secondary schools, compared with core programs in every school.
issues.whatItAffects: Secondary students, families choosing programs, local employers and post-secondary partners.
issues.whoDecides: The board decides which specialized and career programs to offer, where, and how they are funded within its budget.

viewQuestion.question: How should the district balance specialized programs and core programs?
viewQuestion.poleA: Expand programs of choice and career pathways such as trades and academies
viewQuestion.poleB: Focus resources on core programs available at every neighbourhood school

tradeoffs.context: Program choices trade specialized and career options against stronger core programs at every school.

gains: Students may get more paths into trades and post-secondary
Partnerships may connect students with local employers
costs: Costs and seats may favour students who can travel or apply
Less funding may be left for neighbourhood schools

gains: All students may get similar programs close to home
Funding may stay focused on core learning
costs: Fewer specialized options may be available
Some students may look elsewhere for programs they want

issues.title: Board accountability and transparency
issues.description: How openly the SD43 board makes and explains decisions on budgets and planning, and how closely it works with Port Moody council, after disagreements over the school site plan.
issues.whatItAffects: Parents, students, staff, and Port Moody residents and council.
issues.whoDecides: The board sets its own meeting, consultation and reporting practices and decides how it works with city councils.

viewQuestion.question: How should the board engage the public and the city?
viewQuestion.poleA: Expand public consultation and joint planning with the city before major decisions
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep consultation focused and let the board and staff move decisions forward on schedule

tradeoffs.context: Engagement choices trade broader consultation and joint planning against keeping decisions on schedule.

gains: Parents and cities may better understand board decisions
Joint planning may reduce conflicts over growth
costs: Decisions may take longer to reach
Consultation may add staff time and costs

gains: Decisions such as budgets may stay on schedule
Staff time may stay focused on schools
costs: Some families may feel less involved
Disagreements with cities may surface later

election.name: School District 43 (Coquitlam) trustee election
election.appliesTo: Port Moody voters elect 2 of School District 43's 9 trustees (Coquitlam 4, Port Coquitlam 2, Port Moody 2, Anmore/Belcarra 1). Anmore and Belcarra form their own separate trustee area. Port Moody's trustee vote is run by the City alongside the municipal election, at the same places and times; non-resident property electors living in Coquitlam, Port Coquitlam, Anmore or Belcarra cannot vote for Port Moody trustees.
